title: Alternatives to Venice: 5 quieter places with the same magic
author: Brogan
intro: If Venice feels too crowded or too expensive, Piran, Trieste, Verona, Bologna and Ljubljana give you canals, Venetian squares, river bridges or arcaded streets with a fraction of the crowds. Here's how they compare.
seo_description: Piran has Venetian squares by the sea, Trieste a Grand Canal and coffee houses, Verona and Bologna Italian old towns, Ljubljana river bridges. Compared.

sections.heading: The short answer
sections.text:
- **Most like Venice:** Piran, in Slovenia
- **A canal and a sea view:** Trieste
- **Romance and opera:** Verona
- **Food and arcades:** Bologna
- **River bridges, no cars:** Ljubljana

Nothing quite matches Venice, a city built on water with no roads at all. But several places nearby share its history, its look or its slow, walkable feel, without the day-tripper crowds. Most are an easy add-on to a Venice trip, too.

sections.heading: How they compare
sections.text:
| Place | Like Venice because | Fly to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Piran](/destinations/piran) | Venetian-built old town on the sea | Trieste or Ljubljana |
| [Trieste](/destinations/trieste) | A grand canal and a seafront square | Trieste |
| [Verona](/destinations/verona) | Palaces, a river and Venetian lions | Verona |
| [Bologna](/destinations/bologna) | Medieval towers and hidden canals | Bologna |
| [Ljubljana](/destinations/ljubljana) | Bridges over a river, a car-free centre | Ljubljana |

Venice also now charges day-trippers an access fee on busy days: in 2026, €5 or €10 on 60 days between April and July, though overnight guests are exempt. These alternatives charge nothing of the kind.

sections.heading: Piran: the closest match
sections.text:
[Piran](/destinations/piran) is a small town on a finger of land on Slovenia's short coast, and for centuries it was part of the Venetian Republic. You can see it everywhere: in the pastel houses, the narrow lanes and the bell tower of St George's Church, modelled on the campanile in St Mark's Square.

Local knowledge: climb the bell tower of St George's Church for the best view in town, over the red roofs to the sea and, on a clear day, the mountains beyond.

The heart of the town is **Tartini Square**, an oval square that was once the inner harbour, opening on to the sea. Walk the old town walls at sunset for the view over the rooftops, then eat seafood by the water. It's small enough to see in a day, so most people stay two or three nights and add the salt pans at Sečovlje or a day in Trieste, about an hour away by road.

sections.heading: Trieste: canal, coffee and sea
sections.text:
[Trieste](/destinations/trieste) is the most surprising of the five. It was the Habsburg empire's great port, so it feels part Italian, part Austrian. Its **Canal Grande** runs straight into the city, lined with old warehouses and cafés, and **Piazza Unità d'Italia** is a vast square open to the sea on one side.

Trieste is famous for coffee, with grand historic cafés where writers like James Joyce once sat. **Miramare Castle**, a white palace on the shore, makes a lovely walk along the coast.

Tip: Trieste is about two hours from Venice by train, so you can see Venice in a day trip and sleep somewhere calmer and cheaper.

sections.heading: Verona and Bologna: Italian old towns without the queues
sections.text:
[Verona](/destinations/verona) was ruled by Venice for nearly 400 years, and the winged lion of St Mark still stands on a column in **Piazza delle Erbe**. It has a Roman arena that hosts opera in summer, the Adige river curling around the old town, and Juliet's balcony. It's about an hour from Venice by train, and [Lake Garda](/destinations/lake-garda) is close by.

[Bologna](/destinations/bologna) is a food city first: tortellini, ragù and mortadella, eaten under miles of arcaded streets. It hides its own canals, too. Look through the little window in Via Piella and you'll see a canal between old houses that could be in Venice. Both are busy cities with real local life, so they don't empty out at night the way central Venice does.

sections.heading: Ljubljana: the calm capital
sections.text:
[Ljubljana](/destinations/ljubljana), Slovenia's capital, has no lagoon, but its river, the Ljubljanica, is lined with cafés and crossed by beautiful bridges, including the Triple Bridge. The centre is car-free, so it has the same unhurried feel as Venice's quieter corners.

- **A castle on the hill**, reached by funicular or a short walk
- **[Lake Bled](/destinations/lake-bled)**, less than an hour away
- **Piran**, about two hours away, for a week in Slovenia

sections.heading: When Venice is still the right choice
sections.text:
If you've never been, Venice is worth seeing at least once, and there are ways to make it calmer. Stay overnight rather than visiting for the day, explore early in the morning, and pick a quieter month. Our post on the [quietest time to visit Venice](/blog/quietest-time-to-visit-venice) explains when.

Or combine them: two nights in [Venice](/destinations/venice), then the train to Trieste or Verona. Browse the [holidays in Italy](/destinations/holidays-in-italy) page for more. If you can't decide, add a few of these to somewhere.party and let the draw choose.

faqs.question: Where is like Venice but less crowded?
faqs.answer: Piran in Slovenia is the closest match, with a Venetian-built old town by the sea. Trieste, Verona, Bologna and Ljubljana also share some of Venice's look and feel with far fewer visitors.

faqs.question: Do you have to pay to enter Venice in 2026?
faqs.answer: Day-trippers pay an access fee of €5 or €10 on 60 busy days between April and July 2026. Overnight guests are exempt.

faqs.question: How far is Trieste from Venice?
faqs.answer: About two hours by train, which makes it a good base for a day trip to Venice.

faqs.question: Is Piran worth visiting?
faqs.answer: Yes. It's one of the prettiest towns on the Adriatic, with Venetian squares and lanes on the sea. It's small, so two or three nights is enough.
